semantic_correction.stem: A client with alcohol-associated cirrhosis says, "I've cut back, so I don't think I need to stop drinking completely." Which response by the nurse is most accurate?

options.A: Complete abstinence is the treatment goal; the care team can support cessation with counseling and, when appropriate, medications while assessing withdrawal risk.
options.B: Reducing alcohol intake is sufficient once cirrhosis is established, because complete abstinence no longer changes progression of alcohol-related liver injury.
options.C: Alcohol-focused counseling should wait until a formal alcohol use disorder diagnosis is documented, even when cirrhosis is already alcohol-associated.
options.D: Plan abrupt unsupervised cessation without assessing prior withdrawal history, and evaluate withdrawal risk later if symptoms develop after alcohol is stopped.

semantic_correction.rationale: A is correct. Current AASLD clinical guidance states that abstinence from alcohol is the only available treatment that prevents progression of alcohol-related liver injury and that supporting alcohol cessation is first-line therapy for alcohol-associated liver disease. AASLD also describes effective pharmacologic treatment for alcohol use disorder and emphasizes screening for risk of severe alcohol withdrawal when alcohol use is abruptly reduced or stopped. B is incorrect because continued alcohol exposure can continue to drive alcohol-related liver injury after cirrhosis develops; reduction is not equivalent to the abstinence goal described by AASLD. C is incorrect because people with risky alcohol use or alcohol-associated liver disease can benefit from intervention even when a formal alcohol use disorder diagnosis has not yet been established. D is incorrect because severe alcohol withdrawal can be life-threatening, and AASLD advises assessment of withdrawal-risk factors before or during cessation planning rather than waiting for symptoms to emerge.
semantic_correction.educational_objective: Counsel clients with alcohol-associated cirrhosis that abstinence is the treatment goal for preventing further alcohol-related liver injury and that cessation planning should include evidence-based support and assessment of alcohol-withdrawal risk.

semantic_correction.source_locator: Why should hepatologists be involved in treating alcohol use disorder? — first ALD subsection: abstinence from alcohol is the only available treatment to prevent progression of alcohol-related liver injury and supporting alcohol cessation is first-line therapy for ALD. Alcohol Withdrawal Syndrome — patients abruptly decreasing alcohol can develop withdrawal; severe withdrawal can be life-threatening; clinicians should screen for high-risk features and refer for addiction-medicine management when severe-withdrawal risk is high. Conclusions/Key Points — pharmacotherapy can support AUD treatment; abstinence prevents progression of alcohol-related liver injury.
semantic_correction.source_claim_supported: AASLD supports abstinence as the treatment goal that prevents progression of alcohol-related liver injury, use of evidence-based AUD treatment including medications when appropriate, and assessment of alcohol-withdrawal risk during cessation planning.

audit_findings_append.finding: The revised item tests abstinence-focused counseling in alcohol-associated cirrhosis while preserving safe withdrawal-risk assessment, with one clearly best answer and no conspicuous cueing.

option_audit.A: Correct. AASLD directly supports abstinence as first-line ALD therapy, evidence-based AUD treatment, and withdrawal-risk assessment when alcohol use is reduced or stopped.
option_audit.B: Incorrect. It substitutes partial reduction for the abstinence goal that AASLD identifies as the intervention preventing progression of alcohol-related liver injury.
option_audit.C: Incorrect. AASLD notes that people with risky alcohol use can benefit from intervention even when screening tools have not established a formal AUD diagnosis.
option_audit.D: Incorrect. Severe alcohol withdrawal can be life-threatening, and AASLD advises screening for severe-withdrawal risk rather than deferring risk assessment until symptoms occur.

ambiguity_check: No second defensible answer. A alone combines the abstinence goal with appropriate treatment support and withdrawal-risk assessment; B accepts continued alcohol exposure, C improperly delays intervention, and D delays withdrawal-risk assessment until after cessation.
cueing_check: The choices are closely balanced in length and all are framed as management recommendations; the prior correct-answer length advantage and conspicuous absolute-word distractor wording were removed.
